keyVerseText: And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.
rootMeaning: The name מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (Malkîy-Tsedeq) combines two Hebrew roots: מֶלֶךְ (melek), meaning 'king,' and צֶדֶק (tsedeq), meaning 'right' or 'righteousness.' Literally, the name can be understood as 'my king is righteousness' or 'king of right.' This etymology enriches the common English gloss 'Melchizedek' by emphasizing a royal figure whose authority is inherently tied to justice and righteousness, highlighting a divine or moral kingship rather than mere political power.
usageInScripture: The term מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק appears only twice in Scripture, consistently referring to the same individual: the king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. The top translations include 'And Melchizedek' and 'of Melchizedek,' indicating its use primarily as a proper name rather than a title. This consistency underscores the uniqueness and importance of this figure in biblical narrative, especially as a priest-king who intersects royal and priestly roles.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק as 'king of righteousness' is crucial for grasping the biblical portrayal of priesthood and kingship united in one person, which prefigures Christ’s eternal priesthood. Melchizedek’s dual role as king and priest points to a divine order beyond the Levitical priesthood, often called 'the order of Melchizedek,' to which Christ belongs. This highlights Christ’s superior and eternal priesthood, combining righteous kingship with intercessory ministry, affirming his unique role in salvation history. The name itself invites believers to trust in a sovereign ruler whose reign is founded on perfect righteousness.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 14:18 states, 'And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.' Here, the name מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק anchors the identity of this mysterious figure as both king and priest, emphasizing his authority and righteousness. The verse’s mention of bread and wine also foreshadows Christ’s priestly ministry and covenant, deepening the understanding of Melchizedek as a typological precursor to Jesus, who embodies the perfect 'king of righteousness' and eternal priest.
